summary: This informational memo discusses mobility in Nimrod, an experimental routing architecture. Mobility is not built into Nimrod, so the document lists what Nimrod needs from any solution and compares existing approaches, with their advantages and disadvantages.

eli5.summary: If a friend keeps moving house, you need a way to still find them. This note compares ways to do that.

questions: how can routing support mobile hosts
how to support mobile devices in routing
subtitle: What a routing architecture needs to support mobile endpoints.

tldr.problem: As portable devices become common, routers need to handle endpoints that move and change their network location, but Nimrod, an experimental routing architecture, did not specify how to support mobility.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists what Nimrod requires from any mobility solution and compares existing approaches, including home-representative schemes and IETF Mobile-IP, showing how each handles the dynamic mapping between endpoint identity and network location.
tldr.outcome: Nimrod remains flexible by allowing multiple mobility approaches as long as they meet its requirements. The document demonstrates how Mobile-IP can be implemented within Nimrod using its address and location separation.

facts.value: 4 (no change, locator change, topology change, both change)

facts.label: Key Nimrod feature for mobility
facts.value: Separation of endpoint identity from locator

today: RFC 2103 is informational and has not been obsoleted. While Nimrod was an experimental architecture that did not see wide deployment, Mobile-IP became an important real-world protocol for supporting mobile devices in IP networks. The fundamental insights about separating identity from location remain relevant to modern mobility solutions.

sections.title: Mobility in Nimrod
sections.content:
Mobility is the ability of endpoints (computers, networks, or devices) to change their physical location and network attachment point while remaining reachable. As wireless and portable networking became more important, supporting mobility became essential for any future routing architecture. Nimrod, like with multicast, does not specify a particular mobility solution. Instead, it defines what characteristics any solution must have and evaluates existing approaches.

The document lists requirements that Nimrod places on mobility support and compares five different approaches. It then shows concretely how IETF's Mobile-IP protocol—being developed in parallel by the Mobile-IP working group—could be implemented within Nimrod's architecture. The key insight is that Nimrod separates endpoint naming from locator addressing, which naturally supports mobility.
sections.eli5: Nimrod says 'we don't care how you track moving people, as long as you do it efficiently.' This document explains why that's hard and which techniques could work.

sections.title: Identity Versus Location
sections.content:
A core feature of Nimrod is the separation between endpoint identity and locator. An endpoint has a globally unique endpoint identifier (EID) and an endpoint label (EL) that remain the same throughout its life. A locator specifies where the endpoint is attached to the network topology. When an endpoint moves, its EID and EL stay the same, but its locator changes.

This separation is the foundation for mobility support. The document introduces the abstraction of a dynamic association module (DAM) that maintains the mapping between EIDs and locators. Nimrod's routing finds paths to locators, while the DAM tracks where each EID is located. This modular view allows different mobility solutions to be plugged into Nimrod as long as they maintain the EID-to-locator association. The document notes that this is more flexible than simply updating DNS, since the system must track real-time location changes, not just static address assignments.
sections.eli5: Every person has a permanent name (like your Social Security number). Your locator is your current house address. When you move, your name stays the same, but your address changes. The system just needs to keep track of the mapping.

sections.title: How Mobility Affects Routing
sections.content:
Mobility creates different effects depending on what changes. The document identifies four scenarios. First, neither locator nor topology changes—the trivial case where moving within a LAN does not affect routing. Second, the locator changes but topology does not—a host moves to a different subnet. Third, topology changes but locator does not—a mobile network such as one on an airplane moves between cells. Fourth, both change—a mobile network connects to a new part of the Internet.

Each scenario requires different handling. A locator change means the DAM must update its mapping and notify Nimrod to reroute traffic. A topology change means the topology maps used for routing must be updated. A change in both requires both updates. The document notes that mobility does not require modifications to Nimrod's core routing algorithm; it only requires that the DAM and Nimrod coordinate when the EID-locator mapping or topology changes.
sections.eli5: Moving within your home doesn't need the post office to do anything. Moving to a new town means updating your address. If your whole office moves, the Internet needs to know a new building is now connected. These are different problems.

sections.title: Mobility Solution Approaches
sections.content:
The document compares approaches based on where the association between EID and locator is maintained. In DNS-like approaches, a centralized service maps EIDs to locators, but real-time updates and query latency can be problematic. In home-representative approaches, each endpoint has a home location where a representative maintains the mapping. Packets sent to the old locator are intercepted and forwarded to the new one, but this can create inefficient paths.

End-to-end update approaches require the mobile endpoint to actively notify all correspondents of its new locator, but this does not scale for many connections. Hybrid approaches combine centralized registration with efficient forwarding. Sender-side mechanisms place the burden on the sender to track and use current locators. Each approach has trade-offs in scalability, latency, and complexity. Nimrod's flexibility allows different implementations to choose the approach best suited to their deployment.
sections.eli5: You could call everyone and tell them your new address (hard if you know many people), have a home office forward your mail (works but slow), put a sign at your old address telling delivery people where you moved (not reliable), or have a central registry everyone checks (like phonebook, but updated in real time).

sections.title: Implementing Mobile-IP in Nimrod
sections.content:
Mobile-IP, being developed by the IETF's Mobile-IP working group, provides a concrete example of how mobility can work in Nimrod. In Mobile-IP, each endpoint is associated with a home network. When the endpoint moves, it obtains a temporary locator called a care-of-address at its new location. A home agent on the home network maintains the mapping and intercepts traffic sent to the home address, tunneling it to the care-of-address.

This approach fits naturally into Nimrod. The home agent maintains the EID-to-locator mapping (the DAM functionality). Nimrod's routing delivers traffic using locators. When an endpoint moves and obtains a new care-of-address, the home agent updates the mapping, and Nimrod routes traffic accordingly. The document demonstrates that Nimrod's separation of identity from location and its flexible forwarding modes make it well-suited to supporting Mobile-IP-style mobility.
sections.eli5: You have a permanent home address. When you travel, you get a temporary address at your current location. Your home office keeps track and forwards important mail to wherever you are. That simple idea is what Mobile-IP does.
